situation:
You are the finance manager at BRIGHTWATER ANIMAL HOSPITALS, a network of six veterinary clinics in one metropolitan area. The founding veterinarian (judge), who opened the first clinic and is preparing to retire at the end of next year, has asked you to recommend whether the network should refinance the loan it took out to build its sixth clinic.

BRIGHTWATER ANIMAL HOSPITALS is profitable, and its exam rooms are booked to the last appointment hour six days a week. The clinics also stock prescription diet food, and a share of every order expires on the shelf before the client it was stocked for comes back for it. The loan the network carries today has a variable rate that has risen twice this year.

A regional bank has offered to refinance the loan at a lower fixed rate. Refinancing at the lower fixed rate cuts the monthly payment and holds it for eight years, and the bank's terms require the network to close the overnight emergency service, which is full most nights and is where the network's longest-standing clients bring their animals at two in the morning.

Keeping the variable-rate loan and the overnight emergency service keeps those longest-standing clients, and it keeps the prescription diet food moving through the night shift instead of expiring on the shelf, and it leaves the monthly payment exposed to a rate that has risen twice this year and would take the sixth clinic's cash cushion with it if it rises again.

The founding veterinarian (judge) wants your analysis of what each loan does to the network's cash, a view on what the network does about the prescription diet food that expires on the shelf under either one, and a recommendation on how the decision is explained to the clients it touches. The founding veterinarian (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
